evidence: One reference. It has public numbers (1,938,059 views, 5,421 likes, 89 comments, a 700-follower channel, as of 2026-11-25) but one video gives no result evidence: these are what the reference does, not proof of what performs. The reference is NOT a lyric video: it is one still title card held for 185.33 s under a full song, with no lyric on screen at any time, no motion and no cut. Every value about how lyrics are set, timed, moved or coloured is therefore null, and the brief governs those. Tool figures are given as measured; ranged values are the single reference's figure widened about 15% either way; length follows the brief (20 to 30 s), not the reference (185.33 s). Sung-word figures rest on a low-trust transcript of singing over a band.

hook.type: a complete title card at frame 0: the song's one-word title in the only colour on the page, beside a stippled ink drawing of two crying eyes; no sung word and no motion in the first 3 s
hook.question_opened: none in words in the first 3 s; the song's own question, 'does the person stay?', opens with the first sung line at 13.4 s

lyric_lines.source: analyst's count from the sound, plus or minus 0.3 s; not a tool figure

structure.does: 0.00-13.36 s: title and credit on screen, quiet instrumental, no voice. A fault at the brief's length: do not copy
13.4-33.3 s: six lines. The plea is sung and repeated at once (13.4, 16.8 s); the consequence line follows at 23.7 s. Opens the question 'does the person stay?'
34.2-55.6 s: the same two lines again, six times between them, now over the full backing (in from about 30 s, level up about 4 dB)
55.6-69.3 s: no voice found by any run, picture unchanged. Do not copy
69.3-89.7 s: verse 2, six new lines of 4 to 6 words. The question appears to be answered at about 73-77 s (the person has gone; tentative). The title word is apparently first sung at about 87-90 s
90.3-107.5 s: the full refrain, first over a thinned backing (90-100 s), then full
107.5-132.4 s: level drops to the quietest point after the intro (110-125 s); four bridge lines at 117.8-132.4 s, the last two a matched pair
132.4-137.4 s: no voice found. Do not copy
137.4-155.9 s: three new lines, then the refrain's two lines again
155.9-168.0 s: no voice found by any run, the most bass-heavy stretch, picture unchanged. Do not copy
168.0-182.9 s: two long lines of about 11 words, about 7.4 s each, addressed to the one who left, over a thinned backing
182.9-185.33 s: sound fades, 1.72 s of silence on the unchanged card. No end card. Do not copy

share_triggers: the words are addressed to 'you', so sending the song says them to someone (refrain at 13.4 and 23.7 s, closing lines at 168.0-182.9 s; 5 of 75 comments tell their own loss or dedicate the song to a person)
one plain feeling that needs no context: being left (30 of 75 comments carry a crying, sad or broken-heart emoji)
a line people single out: 4 of 75 comments point to a moment by time (1:50, 1:15, 1:06, 0:02-0:22)
not a trigger: the picture. 0 of 75 comments mention it
comment_triggers: the song itself draws short praise: 34 of 75 comments are praise in words, 20 are emoji only; the three most-liked (19, 18, 13 likes) are plain praise
a subject wide enough for the viewer's own story: 5 of 75 tell one or dedicate the song
a favourite line or passage to point at: 4 of 75 are timestamps
the writing: 2 of 75 praise it, one with an aphorism of the viewer's own (6 likes)
nothing in the video asks for a reply: no question, claim or prompt, and no comment asks or disputes anything; 89 comments on 1.94 million views

sound.music: a full song: sung voice over instruments for the whole run, no silence between lines (audible share 0.988); character and instruments not measurable

look.accent_means: the song's title: one word, the only coloured thing in the frame, about 1.2% of its area
look.style: stippled ink drawing (two crying eyes, no face) on cream paper with faint creases and rain-like dashes; one large brushed word in dark red on the left, the drawing on the right, about 94% of the frame left as paper; nothing moves

notes.reference_is_lyric_video: Every one of the reference's 5,560 frames was compared with frame 0 at full size: the picture is one still image from 0.00 to 185.33 s. The only on-screen words are a one-word title and a one-word credit. The judges cannot hold our lyric setting, timing, motion or colour to this reference; a reference that shows lyrics on screen would be needed for that.
notes.format.width: 640x360 is the size of the supplied file, a low-bitrate rendition (about 32 kb/s of video); the upload's own size is not known (info.json has no width or height). Hold our video to horizontal 16:9, not to this pixel count. compare.py passes any height of 360 or more.
notes.format.duration_s: The brief's value. The reference runs 185.33 s (picture) and 185.48 s (sound).
notes.hook.first_word_s: Not a measurement. The reference's first sung word is at 13.36 s (tool; three models agree), which is 7.2% of its 185.33 s. The brief's length wins, and the same share of 20 to 30 s is 1.4 to 2.2 s: that scaled range is the value given. A 13.36 s wait is listed as a fault and must not be copied. compare.py compares with 13.36 s plus or minus 0.4 and will fail our video on this row by construction: disregard that row.
notes.hook.words_in_first_3s: Tool figure: 0 sung words before 3 s. On screen there are 2 words from 0.00 s (analyst's count), neither of them a lyric.
notes.hook.first_cut_s: The reference has no cut at all (tool and eye agree).
notes.hook.question_opened: The analyst's reading. The picture (title 'rain', crying eyes) implies 'who is crying and why' but states nothing.
notes.hook.works_muted: The brief's requirement (the words appear on screen in time with the voice; the lyrics are the picture), not the reference's behaviour. In the reference the first frame reads muted as a title card, but none of the roughly 160 sung words is ever shown, so over the run it does not work muted.
notes.pacing.words_per_minute: Tool figure 39 (transcribe.py, medium model, language set to Hindi), widened 15%. It is an undercount and not a usable budget: the tool's voice-activity filter dropped sung passages at about 50-88 s, 132-154 s and 155-172 s, and the other two tool runs gave 36 (base) and 30 (small). Analyst's count: about 160 words, about 52 a minute over the run, and that still includes about 57 s with no voice (intro and breaks), which are faults. For the script, budget from lyric_lines instead: 6 to 8 line slots of about 4 words, 24 to 32 words in 20 to 30 s (about 64 to 72 a minute). A script written to that budget will exceed this field and compare.py's 'words a minute, whole run' row (target 33 to 45): that is expected, not a defect.
notes.pacing.speaking_rate_wpm: Tool figure 96, widened 15%; 95 and 75 in the other two tool runs. It is a sung pace measured on the fragments the tool caught. Analyst's count inside the sung stretches, on a looser definition that keeps the short gaps between lines: about 75. The brief's voice is spoken, not sung (accepted by the user for this test), so a natural spoken pace will sit above this range and each line will be shorter than its 3.5 s slot; whether to slow the voice or let the bed fill the slot is the producer's decision. compare.py's 'while speaking' row (target about 84 to 108) will fail a normally paced spoken voice.
notes.pacing.mean_shot_s: The reference is one unbroken shot: tool figure 185.33 s, the whole run. The brief's length wins, so one unbroken shot is 20 to 30 s. compare.py compares with 185.33 s ('mean shot length' target about 130 to 241 s, 'longest shot' about 120 to 250 s) and will fail both rows on length alone: disregard them.
notes.pacing.cuts_per_10s: Tool figure 0.0 (no widening: 15% of zero is zero). It records that the reference never cuts; it is not evidence that a lyric video should not. The reference shows nothing about changing the picture between sections. compare.py fails any cut at all against 0; if the producer cuts or changes the ground between sections, weigh that row against the brief.
notes.pacing.longest_still_s: Tool figure 7.0 s, and an artefact: the file has a keyframe every 7.0 s and each one redraws the same image slightly differently, which breaks the tool's stillness test. By eye and by full-size frame comparison the picture is still for the whole 185.33 s. That stillness is a fault. Treat 7.0 s as the most the comparison will tolerate, not as a target: with a new line about every 3.5 s and words that follow the voice, our longest frozen stretch should be far shorter.
notes.pacing.end_hold_s: Tool figure 3.33 s, the time since the last keyframe at 182.0 s; an artefact for the same reason. By sound: the last sung word ends at 182.3 to 182.9 s and the file ends at 185.33 s, so the unchanged card runs 2.4 to 3.0 s past the last word, the final 1.72 s in silence (tool: tail_silence). The reference has no end card.
notes.pacing.payoff_at_share_of_run: Null: no payoff could be fixed. The reference is a song with a returning refrain, not a story with a reveal, and the reading of its words rests on a low-trust transcript. Tentatively, the question opened at 13.4 s ('does the person stay?') is answered at about 73-77 s, 0.40 of the run, when a verse line says the person has gone; the refrain returns four more times after that. The title word is apparently first sung at about 87-90 s (0.47). Neither is firm enough to hold our video to.
notes.pacing.still_share: Tool figure. compare.py passes any still share up to 1.0 against this reference, so the tool cannot catch a frozen video here: the judges must check by eye that the words change with the voice.
notes.pacing.motion_mean: Tool figure; the 0.01 is keyframe refresh, not motion. Nothing in the reference moves, which is a fault. Our video's words must appear in time with the voice, so a higher figure is expected. compare.py's two motion rows pass up to about 0.3 and warn up to about 0.6; a result above that is not by itself a defect.
notes.lyrics_on_screen: All null because the reference never shows a lyric. These are the questions the brief asks and the reference cannot answer. Do not fill them from this file.
notes.lyric_lines: The analyst's count from word times in five transcription runs (three tool runs, two cross-checks with the voice-activity filter off). Line starts are good to about 0.3 s. 21 intervals between line starts were measured (13.4-52.0 s, mean 3.51 s; 69.3-104.5 s, mean 3.53 s). 'voiced_part_of_slot_s' is how long the singing lasts within a slot. 'slots_at_brief_length' and 'word_budget_at_brief_length' are arithmetic on those figures at 20 to 30 s, not things the reference does. The closing lines (168.0-182.9 s) are about 11 words over two slots each and fall outside 'words_per_line'.
notes.structure: Shares of the reference's 185.33 s, read from the sound only; the picture marks none of these sections. 'copy': false marks parts listed as faults (the intro before the voice, the voiceless breaks, the fade). A 20 to 30 s video has 6 to 8 line slots and cannot hold this structure; the roles marked true show the order the reference uses (refrain first, repeated; new lines; refrain back; direct closing lines), not lengths to reproduce.
notes.sound.integrated_lufs: Tool figure, not widened: compare.py holds our video to this plus or minus 1.5 LU (-14.3 to -11.3 LUFS). By section (analyst's RMS): intro 0-13 s about -23.5 dB, full sections about -11 dB, thinned sections -13 to -15 dB.
notes.sound.voice: Sung in the reference. Ours is spoken by a synthetic voice by the brief's choice. Tone of voice is not measurable here.
notes.sound.music: The brief forbids reusing the song or recording. What transfers is that the backing never drops out between lines.
notes.sound.cuts_on_sound_share: Null: the reference has no cuts, so measure.json's sync is null. No evidence either way on whether a change of words should land on a sound.
notes.look.ink: Tool figure, the darkest value in the frame. The small type and the drawing average nearer #150a07 to #1a0e06 on a full-size still.
notes.look.accent: Tool figure. The title's pixels average about #821817 on a full-size still.
notes.look.main_type_height_share: Estimates from pixel boxes on a 640x360 still (still_120.jpg): the title is 51 px tall (head-line to baseline) and 178 px wide, centred at about 27% across and 40% down. It is a title, not a lyric; whether lyric lines should take this size and place is the moodboard's decision.
notes.look.style: The brief forbids reusing the reference's artwork. These describe its rules, not a picture to reproduce.
notes.share_triggers: Comment counts are evidence (75 of the platform's 89 comments, hand-sorted). What they say about why people share is the analyst's reading. Share counts are not published.
notes.compare.py: Rows that will mislead against this reference, with the reason in the notes above: 'mean shot length', 'longest shot' and 'first word' fail on the length difference alone; 'cuts per 10 s' fails on any cut; 'words a minute, whole run' and 'words a minute, while speaking' compare a spoken script with an undercounted sung one; 'still picture share' cannot fail; the two motion rows measure against a picture that never moves.
